title: Architecture & Standards: API, Coding, Infra, Model-Serving, Observability, Performance, and ADRs
author: Asha Raman
body:
Overview

This document consolidates Redwood Inference's canonical architecture and standards across API design, coding practices, infrastructure (IaC and networking), model-serving, observability, performance SLOs, and a short ADR registry. The goal is to provide a single reference for engineers building production services that integrate with the Redwood platform and for internal platform components.

Scope

- Audience: backend engineers, platform engineers, infra, SRE, and technical product owners.
- Applies to: new services (internal and customer-facing), model-serving components, CI/CD pipelines, and infra modules.
- Out of scope: one-off experimental notebooks and personal repo prototypes (use team wiki for that).

High-level principles

1) Predictability: APIs and deployments must provide predictable latency and error characteristics; document SLOs and fallbacks.
2) Consistency: follow a small set of conventions for routing, auth, and telemetry to simplify cross-team tooling.
3) Observability-first: every service must emit structured logs, request-level traces, and service metrics before being allowed into production.
4) Security and compliance: encryption-in-transit and at-rest, RBAC for privileged operations, and audit logging for customer-sensitive flows.
5) Incremental rollouts: use canary/A-B rollouts with automatic rollback criteria defined in rollout policy docs.

1) API Standards

Purpose: reduce integration friction, improve client expectations, and make versioning and backward compatibility explicit.

Naming and versioning

- Base path: /v{major}/{resource} (e.g., /v1/generate, /v2/embeddings). Major versions only change for incompatible contract changes.
- Keep minor and patch-level changes backward compatible. Use media type versioning for schema evolution when necessary.

Endpoints and patterns

- Use RESTful, resource-oriented paths for CRUD-style services. For action endpoints (e.g., infer/generate), use clear verbs: POST /v1/generate, POST /v1/stream-chat.
- For streaming response endpoints, include a non-streaming 200 response for backward compatibility and a streaming Content-Type: text/event-stream or application/x-ndjson.

Auth and rate-limiting

- Auth: Bearer token via Authorization header. OAuth for user-bound flows. For server-to-server calls within our infra, use mTLS and service identity tokens.
- Throttling: implement per-route and per-customer quotas. Default rate limiting policy: 100 req/min per API key, adjustable by tier. Rate-limit headers: X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset.

Idempotency and retries

- POST endpoints that create side-effects must accept Idempotency-Key header to ensure exactly-once semantics for client retries.
- Retries: clients should retry idempotent requests on 5xx and 429 with exponential backoff and jitter. Circuit-breakers at the client and service layer required for cascading-failure protection.

Errors and status codes

- Use standard HTTP codes. Include structured error body: {"code": "string", "message": "human", "details": {}}. Standard error codes: INVALID_ARGUMENT, UNAUTHENTICATED, PERMISSION_DENIED, NOT_FOUND, RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED, INTERNAL, UNAVAILABLE, RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED, MODEL_NOT_AVAILABLE.

Pagination and partial results

- Cursor-based pagination preferred for large result sets. Responses include next_cursor. For long-running tasks, return 202 Accepted with a Location header to poll status.

Schema and contract management

- JSON Schema v2020-12 for input/output contracts. Store canonical schemas in the schemas/ directory of the repo and publish to the internal schema registry. All breaking changes require a documented ADR and 2-week migration path.

API example (generation request)

POST /v1/generate
Authorization: Bearer <token>
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "model": "redwood/gpt-4r",
  "input": "Summarize the following...",
  "max_tokens": 256
}

2) Coding Standards

Purpose: reduce maintenance cost, improve readability, and enable automated quality checks. Applies to services across languages; we maintain language-specific linters and formatters.

General rules

- Use idiomatic, well-maintained frameworks for the language (e.g., FastAPI for Python, Actix/axum for Rust, Spring Boot for Java).
- Enforce formatting and linting pre-commit hooks. Required checks: formatting, static analysis, type checks (mypy/pyright for Python), and dependency vulnerability scan.
- All production code must include unit tests with >70% coverage for critical modules and focused integration tests for service boundaries.
- No TODOs left without an associated ticket and owner.

Error handling and observability

- Surface contextual errors (correlate with trace and request id). Prefer typed error objects over opaque strings.
- Avoid swallowing errors; log and re-raise after adding context where appropriate.

Secrets and configuration

- Do not commit secrets. Use Vault/KMS and environment variables. Configuration should be injected via 12-factor environment variables and validated at startup.

3) Infrastructure Standards (IaC, Networking, Security)

Purpose: reproducible, auditable environments and consistent security posture.

Terraform and modules

- Use centralized Terraform repo structure with reusable modules (network, compute, storage, iam, kms). Modules must be versioned and documented. Module inputs must be explicit; avoid relying on implicit defaults.
- State: remote state with locking (e.g., Terraform Cloud or S3 with DynamoDB).

Networking and VPCs

- Default pattern: hub-and-spoke VPCs. Customer-private workloads run in isolated VPCs for Private deployments. Use VPC peering or private link for platform services.
- Egress controls and firewall policies defined in network module. Use least-privilege security groups and Network ACLs.

Secrets and keys

- KMS for key wrapping; customer-managed CMKs optional for Private deployments. Rotate keys at least annually and on personnel changes.

Compliance and audit

- Centralized audit logging (CloudTrail/Stackdriver/AWS equivalent) and retention policy: default 90 days, extended for regulated customers as needed.

Observed infra config snippet (Terraform example)

module "redwood_vpc" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@internal.redwood.com/terraform-modules/vpc.git//modules/hub"
  name   = "redwood-hub-us-west-2"
  cidr   = "10.0.0.0/16"
}

4) Model-serving Standards

Purpose: ensure high throughput, predictable latency, correct cache behavior, and safe model rollouts.

Model packaging and versioning

- Models are packaged as immutable artifacts with metadata: model_name, model_version, quantization_profile, input_schema_hash, and runtime_compatibility. Store artifacts in the model registry (s3://redwood-models/<model>/).
- Semantic versioning for model code; major version increments for behavior changes that can break consumers.

Runtime & resource configuration

- Provide standardized config files per model with recommended CPU/GPU, batch_size, max_sequence_length, and kv-cache-size. Example keys: runtime_version, preferred_instance_type (g4dn.xlarge / a100-40gb), target_latency_p50/p95.

Caching and batching

- Enable prefix/KV caching for repeated contexts. Batching heuristics must expose parameters for maximum_batch_size and max_wait_ms and be tunable per deployment.

Safety and validation

- All models must pass a safety/eval suite before being allowed in production. Include guardrails for profanity, PII leakage, and hallucination thresholds. Safety tests stored in applied-ml-and-evals/prompt-sets-and-benchmarks.

Operational controls

- Support per-model circuit-breakers and automatic fallback to a lower-cost compatible variant when SLO degradation is detected. Define fallback mappings in model-catalog metadata.

5) Observability Standards

Purpose: make debugging and capacity planning fast and reliable with a consistent telemetry model.

Logging

- Structured JSON logs with the following minimum fields: timestamp (ISO8601), level, service, env, request_id, user_id (if available), model, shard_id, message, error_code. Avoid PII in logs; scrub with redact filters before indexing.

Metrics (Prometheus style)

- Required metrics: request_count, request_duration_seconds (histogram), token_generated_count, model_gpu_utilization, batch_size_distribution, cache_hit_ratio. Use consistent metric names and labels: service, env, region, model, route.

Tracing

- Distributed tracing via OpenTelemetry. All incoming requests must create a trace with spans for ingress, model-infer, kv-cache, and response-serialization. Traces must include http.status_code and sample rate at service level (default 10%).

Dashboards and alerts

- Per-service dashboards: latency p50/p95/p99, error rate, saturation metrics, and business-level KPIs where applicable. Alerting thresholds must be documented in the service runbook and follow SRE guidance (see eng-sre/runbooks).

6) Performance Standards and SLOs

Default SLOs (applies to production-hosted services)

- Availability SLO: 99.95% (monthly) for API control plane endpoints.
- Latency target: generation endpoints p95 <= 300ms for small models (<=2.7B) on hosted tier; p95 <= 800ms for large models (>=70B) on dedicated tier (targets may vary by model and plan and must be listed in the model catalog).
- Error budget policy: 10% of budget used triggers incident readiness; 50% triggers mitigation plan; 100% triggers a postmortem and enforcement action.

Load testing and capacity planning

- New services must include a load test plan (k6/JMeter) and a capacity estimation doc before production launch. Document expected traffic patterns and spike tolerances.

Performance benchmarking

- Use benchmarking-and-perf-suite in eng-serving-runtime with representative prompts. Record p50/p95 and cost-per-token for each model and config; publish results in the model catalog.

7) Decision Records (ADRs) Registry

This section captures high-impact architecture decisions and links to ADRs. ADRs should be short, timestamped, and include context, decision, and consequences. Always reference the ADR in PRs when the change affects compatibility or operations.

Sample ADR summaries

- ADR-2025-03: Runtime kernel selection strategy
  - Decision: runtime will select kernels at startup using a hardware + model heuristic and allow per-deployment overrides.
  - Consequence: improved p95 for long sequences; added complexity in tooling.

- ADR-2025-10: API versioning model
  - Decision: major-path versioning (/v1/) for breaking changes; schema registry for minor compatible changes.

- ADR-2026-02: Default caching strategy for hosted inference
  - Decision: enable prefix caching for short-lived contexts by default; allow opt-out per-route.

How to write an ADR

1. Create a new markdown file under architecture-and-standards/adrs/ with a short id.
2. Include: Title, Date, Status (proposed/accepted/deprecated), Context, Decision, Consequences, Rollout plan.
3. Link the ADR in the service README and include reviewers from infra, platform, and applied-ml as appropriate.

Operational runbook checklist (pre-production)

- Define SLOs and error budget with SRE.
- Confirm metrics/trace/logs are emitted and visible on dashboards.
- Create alerting rules and run a game-day to validate on-call flow.
- Document rollback and canary steps in the service runbook.

Ownership and governance

- Architecture and Standards Steward: Eng Platform (rotating primary: last stewarded by Asha Raman).
- ADR approvers: Eng Platform leads, Eng SRE, and Applied ML lead for model-serving impact.
- Periodic review: complete a standards review every 6 months; record changes as ADRs or updates to this doc.

Change log and maintenance

- This document is updated via pull requests to the architecture-and-standards repo. Significant changes require an ADR and review by the reviewers listed above.

References and related resources

- eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture (runtime design)
- eng-sre/slo-and-error-budgets (SRE policies)
- applied-ml-and-evals/prompt-sets-and-benchmarks (safety and evals)
- eng-infra/terraform-and-iac (Terraform modules)

Appendix: Quick checklists

Service launch checklist (brief)
1. API contract in schema registry.
2. Unit and integration tests passing and coverage validated.
3. Observability: logs, metrics, traces present.
4. Load test plan executed and capacity estimated.
5. ADRs referenced for breaking changes.
6. Security review complete for data handling.

Model-serving quick checklist
1. Model artifact in registry with metadata.
2. Safety/eval suite green.
3. Runtime config validated for batch and cache settings.
4. Fallback mapping configured.
5. Canary rollout plan defined.
